content: The Swab2know project, initiated in 2012 and still ongoing, is managed by the HIV/STI clinic of the Institute of Tropical Medicine in Antwerp. It is supported by various community and prevention organizations. The project employs a secure, encrypted website and uses an HIV testing approach based on self-collected oral fluid samples. It combines outreach HIV testing sessions with a home-sampling method. During outreach sessions, participants complete a self-administered questionnaire to collect epidemiological data. Participants create an online account, self-sample oral fluid, and link their samples to their personal accounts using a unique code. Home sampling involves sending a kit to participants, who then return their samples to the laboratory using a prepaid envelope. Test results are uploaded to the website, and participants are notified via email. They can access their results online or opt for an in-person consultation. Those who do not retrieve their results are reminded via phone or email. Emergency counseling by trained paramedics is available by phone. Participants with reactive results are contacted promptly for counseling and linkage to care, with follow-up conducted after confirmation testing. Approximately 1,000 tests are conducted annually, with a 1% yield of new HIV diagnoses. Most newly diagnosed individuals are successfully linked to specialized care, though concerns about false-reactive results persist. The project demonstrates the value of home-sampling with oral fluid and delayed online result communication in a comprehensive HIV testing strategy. The Lesotho Men’s Clinic at the Maseru Seventh Day Adventist (SDA) Health Center was established in 2017 to attract men and boys to HIV and related health services, including antiretroviral therapy (ART) initiation and screening for tuberculosis and sexually transmitted infections (STIs). Staffed exclusively by male nurses and counselors, the clinic offers male-friendly, integrated services. It operates flexibly, accommodating men’s schedules by providing services after working hours and on weekends. This innovation led to a significant increase in men accessing HIV testing services (HTS), from 744 in 2016 to 2,916 in 2017, with a corresponding rise in positive diagnoses from 84 to 254. Most men testing positive were linked to ART initiation due to Lesotho’s test-and-treat policy. The clinic’s success highlights the importance of tailored approaches to engage men in HIV care. Project Sahay, implemented across six Indian states, aims to identify vulnerable populations and conduct community-based HIV testing to facilitate early ART initiation. The program also links HIV-positive individuals to socioeconomic welfare schemes and enhances access to STI, HIV, and reproductive health services for female partners of men who have sex with men (MSM) and transgender individuals. Between November 2017 and September 2018, over 36,000 people were tested at 717 sites, achieving a 91% linkage to ART for those confirmed positive. The program employs localized strategies, including community-based testing in high-risk areas, and has demonstrated effective mobilization of MSM and transgender populations to HIV services. The Samarth project in India focuses on strengthening the HIV care cascade for MSM, transgender, and hijra populations. It is a community-led HIV screening program that has successfully mobilized these populations to access HIV services. The program has achieved high positivity rates and linkage to ART, serving as a model for scaling up community-based screening nationwide. In Uganda, the HIV/AIDS and Health Initiatives in Workplaces Activity (HIWA) project, funded by USAID, aims to scale up comprehensive HIV/AIDS services for workers and their families. The project established a 24/7 call center staffed by medical professionals to provide health information, counseling, and referrals. In 2018, over 13,500 beneficiaries were reached through mobile messaging, with 97% completing the referral process. The project has improved access to HIV services for men and their families through virtual and workplace-based interventions. One Tent Health, based in Washington, DC, provides rapid HIV screening in underserved communities using a small tent set up at community hubs. The organization targets high-prevalence areas and partners with local health facilities for linkage to care. Services are free and accessible, with rapid test results available in 15 minutes. The program has achieved high client satisfaction and effective linkage to care and prevention services. The Sisli Health Clinic in Istanbul, Turkey, integrates HIV services into primary healthcare, offering stigma-free care to all populations, including LGBTQI individuals and refugees. Funded by municipal taxes, the clinic provides free HIV services and uses an electronic coding system to maintain client confidentiality. The program has strong ties with community-based organizations and serves as a model for integrating HIV services into municipal health clinics across Turkey. The Zindagi project in Pakistan delivers harm reduction and HIV services to drug users and their spouses. Female outreach workers provide HIV testing, counseling, and linkage to care in the privacy of clients’ homes. The program has demonstrated the feasibility of delivering community-based services to this vulnerable population, achieving high rates of testing and ART linkage. In Zimbabwe, the Going the Last Mile for HIV Control program focuses on identifying new HIV-positive clients, linking them to treatment, and retaining them in care. Enhanced peer mobilizers are trained to reach key populations, including MSM and female sex workers, with HIV messages and services. The program has achieved high rates of testing, positivity, and ART linkage through community-based index testing and peer-driven strategies. The Assisted Partner Services (aPS) Scale-up Study in Kenya evaluates the integration of aPS into real-world settings. The study involves notifying sexual partners of HIV-positive individuals and offering them testing and care. Early results show high rates of partner testing, positivity, and ART linkage, demonstrating the effectiveness of aPS in identifying and linking HIV-positive men to care.
